Iyer G.lab_name: Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Iyer G.role: Medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering who heads its bladder cancer section and studies the genetics behind how bladder tumors respond to drugs
Iyer G.sub: Section Head, Bladder Cancer, Genitourinary Oncology Service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · Medical Oncology fellowship, Memorial Sloan Kettering · Internal Medicine residency, University of Michigan · MD, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine
story: Gopa Iyer is first author of an Atlas study (IYE2012) that started with one unusual patient. In a clinical trial of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, in advanced bladder cancer, one patient had a complete and unusually long-lasting remission. The team sequenced the whole genome of that patient's tumor and found a mutation that knocks out TSC1. TSC1 is part of the brake that normally keeps mTOR in check, so a tumor without it depends heavily on mTOR and is easy to hit with an mTOR blocker.

The group then checked 109 more bladder tumors and found TSC1 mutations in about 8 percent. In the trial, patients whose tumors carried such mutations tended to do better on everolimus. Because the idea grew from a single patient, the Atlas treats it as a strong hypothesis rather than proof. The paper helped start the practice of studying exceptional responders: sequencing the rare patient for whom a drug works unusually well to learn who else might benefit.

Iyer trained in medicine at Vanderbilt University, did a residency in internal medicine at the University of Michigan, and completed a medical oncology fellowship at Memorial Sloan Kettering. Today Iyer is a genitourinary medical oncologist and early drug development specialist there and heads the bladder cancer section. The research centers on the genetic makeup of bladder cancer through MSK's Bladder Cancer Oncogenome Project, and on clinical trials of new drugs for cancers of the bladder, kidney and prostate.

highlights.IYE2012: First author: led the genome sequencing of an exceptional everolimus responder and the follow-up that linked TSC1 loss to drug sensitivity in bladder cancer.

Iyer G.note: Current title (Section Head, Bladder Cancer) from MSK physician page; training years not given there.

Hennessy-Strahs S.lab_name: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center, Houston Methodist Hospital (Houston, Texas, USA)
Hennessy-Strahs S.role: Researcher who moved from studying heart pumps and blood vessels at Penn to transplant immunology in Houston, and first author of a study showing that the lung's cleaning macrophages need mTOR to survive
Hennessy-Strahs S.sub: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center and Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital, and Texas A&M University College of Medicine (papers 2025–2026) · Texas A&M University (2022 paper) · Division of Cardiovascular Surgery, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (papers 2017–2021)
story: Samson Hennessy-Strahs is first author of an Atlas study (HEN2026) on alveolar macrophages, the immune cells that sit in the tiny air sacs of the lung and swallow up surfactant, the soapy film that keeps the sacs open. In mice, the team removed mTOR only from myeloid cells, the family that includes macrophages. The alveolar macrophages slowly disappeared, the ones left could not eat particles well, fat built up inside them, and the lungs filled with material in a pattern resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a rare human lung disease. Treating normal mice with the mTOR-blocking drug temsirolimus gave a similar picture.

The finding matters because mTOR inhibitors are used in transplant patients and in cancer, and some patients develop lung problems on them. The study suggests one possible reason: the drugs may starve the lung's own cleaning crew. The work was done in mice, so whether the same happens in patients still has to be shown.

The publication record shows two research phases. From 2017 to 2021 Hennessy-Strahs worked in the Division of Cardiovascular Surgery at the University of Pennsylvania, mostly with Carlo Bartoli, on how left ventricular assist devices (mechanical heart pumps) damage blood proteins such as von Willebrand factor and cause abnormal blood vessels in the gut. A 2022 paper lists Texas A&M University. Since 2025 the papers come from Xian C. Li's transplant immunology group at Houston Methodist Hospital, including a 2025 study on reprogramming macrophages to protect heart transplants in mice. The 2026 Atlas paper also lists the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine. No official profile page was found, so the current role could not be confirmed.

highlights.HEN2026: First author: showed in mice that alveolar macrophages need mTOR to survive and that losing it, by gene deletion or the drug temsirolimus, causes a lung disease resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

Hennessy-Strahs S.note: No web profile found; career path built from PubMed affiliations only. Current position not confirmed.

Peng M.lab_name: Peng Lab, School of Medicine, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)
Peng M.role: Immunologist at Tsinghua University who, as a postdoc at Memorial Sloan Kettering, identified Sestrins and SZT2 as brakes on mTORC1 and now studies how T cells grow, specialise and remember
Peng M.sub: Tenured Associate Professor, School of Medicine, Tsinghua University (since 2024) · Associate Professor (2023–2024) and Assistant Professor (2017–2023), Tsinghua University · Research Fellow and Research Associate, Immunology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (2010–2017) · PhD in Immunology, Peking Union Medical College (2010)
story: Min Peng is first author of an Atlas study (PEN2017) about how cells tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that amino acids are scarce. Two protein complexes on the lysosome do this job: GATOR1 switches mTORC1 off, and GATOR2 holds GATOR1 back. The paper showed that a large protein called SZT2 pulls GATOR1 and GATOR2 together into one complex on the lysosome surface. Cells without SZT2 kept mTORC1 switched on even when starved of amino acids, and mice lacking SZT2 died soon after birth. The work, in cells and mice, added SZT2 to the list of parts that let mTORC1 sense nutrients.

Peng studied clinical medicine at Sichuan University and earned a PhD in immunology at Peking Union Medical College in 2010. From 2010 to 2017 Peng worked in the Immunology Program at Memorial Sloan Kettering in New York, in the group of Ming Li, the senior author of the Atlas paper. There Peng also showed that Sestrin proteins act on the Rag GTPases to hold mTORC1 down (Cell, 2014).

In 2017 Peng started a lab at the School of Medicine of Tsinghua University in Beijing and became a tenured associate professor in 2024. The lab studies how T cells, the white blood cells that kill infected and cancerous cells, are activated, divide, specialise and form memory, including the role of metabolism in these steps. It continues the mTOR thread: a 2022 paper from the lab showed that SZT2 keeps blood stem cells in balance by tuning mTORC1 to nutrients. The lab also develops engineered T cell therapies, including a T cell state it calls TIF that can renew itself for a long time while keeping its function.

highlights.PEN2017: First author: showed that SZT2 links GATOR1 and GATOR2 on the lysosome so that mTORC1 shuts off when amino acids run low.

Peng M.note: Postdoc supervisor (Ming Li) inferred from MSK Immunology Program affiliation plus Li as senior author on PEN2017; the Tsinghua page does not name the supervisor.

Foretz M.lab_name: Institut Cochin, Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Inserm (Paris, France)
Foretz M.role: Researcher at the Institut Cochin in Paris who studies how the liver controls sugar and fat, and whose 2010 work showed that metformin can lower liver glucose output without AMPK
Foretz M.sub: Institut Cochin, CNRS, Inserm, Université Paris Cité (papers 2010–2025) · Inserm U465, Centre de Recherches Biomédicales des Cordeliers, Paris (1999 paper)
story: Marc Foretz is first author of an Atlas study (FOR2010) that changed how scientists explain metformin, the most widely used diabetes drug. For years the simple story was that metformin works by switching on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, which then shuts down sugar production in the liver. The team tested this in mice and liver cells that lacked AMPK or its activating kinase LKB1. Metformin still lowered glucose production. Instead, the drug lowered the liver's energy charge, the balance of ATP to its used-up forms, and that alone was enough to slow the making of new glucose.

For the Atlas this matters because metformin is often described as an indirect mTOR blocker acting through AMPK. The paper shows that its main sugar-lowering effect in the liver does not need that route, so any claim that metformin works mainly through AMPK and mTOR needs separate evidence. The experiments were in mice and isolated liver cells.

Foretz has worked on liver metabolism for more than 25 years. A 1999 paper from the Inserm unit at the Centre des Cordeliers in Paris, with Pascal Ferré and Fabienne Foufelle, showed that the transcription factor SREBP-1c carries insulin's message to genes for sugar and fat handling in liver cells. At the Institut Cochin, working closely with Benoit Viollet, Foretz went on to study AMPK and metformin in the liver, and in 2025 co-wrote a major review on how metformin lowers blood sugar. No official profile page could be opened, so the exact current title is not confirmed; the 2025 affiliation is the Institut Cochin.

highlights.FOR2010: First author: showed in mice and liver cells lacking AMPK or LKB1 that metformin still blocks glucose production by lowering the liver's energy charge.

Foretz M.note: Could not open an official CV (HAL CV page blocked). Current title unconfirmed.

Martins-Branco D.lab_name: Scientific and Medical Division, European Society for Medical Oncology (Lugano, Switzerland)
Martins-Branco D.role: Portuguese medical oncologist focused on breast cancer who moved from clinical research at the Institut Jules Bordet to the scientific division of the European Society for Medical Oncology
Martins-Branco D.sub: Scientific and Medical Division, European Society for Medical Oncology, Lugano (2026 paper) · Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Université libre de Bruxelles (papers 2022–2026) · Breast Multidisciplinary Clinic, Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa Francisco Gentil (earlier papers)
story: Diogo Martins-Branco is first author of EVERGREEN (MAR2026), a study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite hormone therapy combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, today's standard first treatment. The question was whether adding everolimus, an mTOR blocker, to the next hormone therapy still helps. Across several centres, patients given everolimus went a little longer before the cancer grew again (median 5.0 versus 4.3 months) but did not clearly live longer.

Everolimus was approved for this kind of breast cancer before CDK4/6 inhibitors existed, so doctors need to know whether it still works after them. EVERGREEN gives a cautious answer: a small benefit, best kept for selected patients. The study looked back at patient records and was not randomised, so differences in who received the drug may have shaped the result.

Martins-Branco trained and worked as a medical oncologist in Lisbon, publishing from the breast clinic of the Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa on topics such as using genomic tests to spare women chemotherapy. From about 2022 the papers list the Academic Trials Promoting Team at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels, which designs and runs large academic breast cancer trials, and work there included reviews on antibody-drug conjugates. A 2026 paper on the ESMO scale for ranking cancer gene targets lists the Scientific and Medical Division of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Lugano, Switzerland, which appears to be the current post.

highlights.MAR2026: First author: led the multicentre EVERGREEN analysis showing a modest progression-free survival gain from everolimus after CDK4/6 inhibitor failure.

de Azambuja E.lab_name: Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Université libre de Bruxelles (Brussels, Belgium)
de Azambuja E.role: Brazilian-born medical oncologist at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels who designs and runs large academic breast cancer trials
de Azambuja E.sub: Head of the Medical Support Team, Academic Trials Promoting Team, Institut Jules Bordet, Brussels · PhD, Université libre de Bruxelles (2015) · PhD, Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil (2007)
story: Evandro de Azambuja is senior author of EVERGREEN (MAR2026), a study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Adding everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, to the next hormone therapy gave a modest delay in cancer growth (median 5.0 versus 4.3 months) without a clear gain in survival. The study used records from several centres and was not randomised, so the result guides careful selection of patients rather than settling the question.

Everolimus reached breast cancer care through the BOLERO-2 trial in 2012, before CDK4/6 inhibitors became standard. EVERGREEN checks whether that old evidence still holds in today's treatment order, which is the kind of practical question academic trial groups exist to answer.

De Azambuja holds a PhD from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul in Porto Alegre, Brazil (2007), and a second PhD from the Université libre de Bruxelles (2015). At the Institut Jules Bordet de Azambuja heads the medical support team of the Academic Trials Promoting Team, a unit that runs international breast cancer trials. The main research interest is the design and conduct of large clinical trials in breast cancer, including studies of HER2-targeted drugs. De Azambuja also serves on the advisory board of the Anticancer Fund.

highlights.MAR2026: Senior author: supervised the multicentre EVERGREEN analysis of everolimus after CDK4/6 inhibitor failure in advanced breast cancer.

Campone M.lab_name: Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest (Saint-Herblain, France)
Campone M.role: Breast cancer oncologist and general director of the Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest, a co-investigator on the BOLERO-2 trial that brought everolimus into breast cancer care
Campone M.sub: General Director, Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest · Professor of Medical Oncology, University of Angers · Head of Breast Cancer and Translational Research, ICO · Deputy President, Unicancer (since 2019) · MD with oncology certificate, University of Nantes (1998)
story: Mario Campone is a co-author on BOLERO-2, the phase 3 trial that showed mTOR matters in a common cancer. In 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer that had grown despite earlier hormone therapy, adding the mTOR blocker everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review, BAS2012). The idea behind it: cancers that escape hormone therapy often switch on mTOR, so blocking mTOR can restore control. The final report (PIC2014) found a median overall survival of 31.0 months with everolimus and 26.6 months without, a difference that was not statistically significant. Together the two papers show both the real benefit and its limit.

Campone qualified in medicine with a certificate in oncology at the University of Nantes in 1998, with training that included the Beatson Institute in Glasgow, and earned a doctorate in life and health sciences in 2010. Campone is professor of medical oncology at the University of Angers and leads breast cancer and translational research at the Institut de Cancérologie de l'Ouest (ICO), and has headed its phase 1 unit for early drug trials. The research covers new breast cancer drugs, why tumors become resistant to treatment, and markers that predict outcome, including the ORPHEO group that Campone set up with the veterinary school of Nantes.

Today Campone is general director of the ICO, one of France's comprehensive cancer centres with sites in Angers and Saint-Herblain near Nantes, and has been deputy president of Unicancer, the French network of cancer centres, since 2019. Campone also sits on the Science and Innovation Panel of the EU Innovative Health Initiative.

highlights.BAS2012: Co-author: took part in BOLERO-2, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus plus exemestane more than doubled progression-free survival in advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author: contributed to the final BOLERO-2 report, which found a 4.4-month longer median survival with everolimus that did not reach statistical significance.

Baur JA.lab_name: Baur Lab, Department of Physiology and Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Baur JA.role: Biologist of aging at the University of Pennsylvania whose lab showed that rapamycin's harm to glucose control comes from mTORC2 loss and studies how NAD levels shape health
Baur JA.sub: Professor of Physiology, Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · postdoc, Paul F. Glenn Laboratories, Harvard Medical School (David Sinclair lab, 2006 paper) · PhD research, Department of Cell Biology, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Woodring Wright and Jerry Shay, 2001 paper)
story: Joseph Baur is senior author of an Atlas study (LAM2012) that solved a puzzle about rapamycin. The drug lengthens life in mice, yet long-term use makes them glucose intolerant and insulin resistant, which looks like early diabetes. The team showed that chronic rapamycin, at doses close to those that extend lifespan, gradually disrupts a second mTOR complex, mTORC2, and that loss of mTORC2 in the liver explains the insulin problem: the liver keeps making glucose when it should stop. Mice with genetically lowered mTORC1 activity lived longer with normal glucose handling. So the longevity benefit and the metabolic side effect can be separated, which opened the search for drugs that hit only mTORC1.

Baur did PhD research in the Department of Cell Biology at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas with Woodring Wright and Jerry Shay, showing in 2001 that genes near telomeres, the ends of chromosomes, are silenced in human cells depending on telomere length. As a postdoc at Harvard Medical School in David Sinclair's lab, Baur was first author of the 2006 Nature paper showing that resveratrol improved health and survival of mice on a high-calorie diet.

Today Baur is professor of physiology at the Perelman School of Medicine and the Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism at the University of Pennsylvania. The lab studies basic mechanisms of aging with two main lines. One is NAD, a molecule every cell needs for energy metabolism; the lab identified SLC25A51 as the transporter that carries NAD into mitochondria. The other is rapamycin, where the lab works to separate its longevity effects from side effects, including showing that its effect on blood fats involves loss of mTORC1 signaling in fat cells.

highlights.LAM2012: Senior author: led the work showing that chronic rapamycin causes insulin resistance through mTORC2 loss, separable from its lifespan benefit.

Baur JA.note: PhD and postdoc labs inferred from first-author papers with UT Southwestern and Harvard affiliations; degree years not confirmed from an official CV.

Scaiola A.lab_name: Ban Lab, Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Scaiola A.role: Structural biologist in Nenad Ban's group at ETH Zurich who solved the 3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and works on how ribosomes are built and how new proteins are processed
Scaiola A.sub: Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2018–2026, Nenad Ban group)
story: Alain Scaiola is first author of the Atlas study SCA2020, a detailed three-dimensional picture of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution, sharp enough to place most individual amino acids. The structure was made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which freezes purified protein complexes in thin ice and combines hundreds of thousands of electron microscope images into one 3D map. mTORC2 is one of the two mTOR complexes and, unlike mTORC1, it is not blocked directly by rapamycin. The map shows why: the tail end of the protein Rictor covers the site on mTOR where the rapamycin-FKBP12 pair would bind.

Scaiola is also a co-author of STU2018, the earlier and lower-resolution architecture of the mTORC2 core (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8). Both papers came from a joint effort of the groups of Timm Maier at the University of Basel and Nenad Ban at ETH Zurich, and they give drug designers an accurate picture of the complex.

Scaiola's publication record from 2018 to 2026 is in Nenad Ban's group at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich. Most of the work is on the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machine: a 2018 first-author structure of a yeast ribosome subunit caught in the last steps of assembly, and later studies with the Deuerling lab in Konstanz on how the NAC complex guides enzymes that trim and tag new proteins as they leave the ribosome (Nature 2024; Nature Communications 2026). No personal web page was found, so the current job title is not confirmed.

highlights.SCA2020: First author: determined the 3.2-angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and showed how Rictor's C-terminus blocks rapamycin binding.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Scaiola A.note: No web profile found (web search budget exhausted during this batch). Current title not confirmed; affiliation ETH Zurich on July 2026 paper.

Aylett CH.lab_name: Aylett Group, Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Aylett CH.role: Structural biologist who solved the first cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1 at ETH Zurich and now leads a cryo-EM group at Imperial College London
Aylett CH.sub: Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology, Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London (papers 2020–2026) · Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2015–2018) · MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (2012 paper with Jan Löwe)
story: Christopher Aylett is first author of AYL2015, the first detailed 3D architecture of human mTORC1, made by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure showed that mTORC1 is a dimer, two copies of mTOR, Raptor and mLST8 joined into a lozenge-shaped complex with the two kinase active sites sitting in deep clefts. That arrangement explains how the complex limits which proteins can reach the active site, and how the drug pair rapamycin-FKBP12 narrows the entrance further. Aylett is also a co-author of STU2018, the matching architecture of the mTORC2 core.

Aylett's earlier work, at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge with Jan Löwe, was on bacterial proteins that push plasmids apart before cell division; a 2012 paper there described a DNA-protein filament at the heart of the TubZRC system. The mTOR structures came from a period at the Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics of ETH Zurich, working with Nenad Ban and Timm Maier.

Since about 2020 Aylett has led a group in the Section for Structural and Synthetic Biology of the Department of Infectious Disease at Imperial College London. The lab uses cryo-EM on large molecular machines, including the unusual RNA polymerase of the giant bacteriophage PhiKZ, a virus being explored as a treatment for Pseudomonas infections (2026), and develops simpler ways to prepare cryo-EM samples, such as a 3D-printed tool for moving fragile carbon and graphene support films.

highlights.AYL2015: First author: determined the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1, a dimer with recessed active sites.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Boehringer D.sub: Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub (CEMK), ETH Zurich (papers since 2020) · Institute of Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (papers 2015–2019)
story: Daniel Boehringer is a co-author on all three Atlas papers that showed the shapes of the two mTOR complexes: the first architecture of human mTORC1 (AYL2015), the architecture of the human mTORC2 core (STU2018), and the 3.2-angstrom structure of mTORC2 (SCA2020). These papers relied on cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM): protein complexes are frozen in a thin layer of ice and imaged many thousands of times, and a computer combines the images into a 3D map. Together they explain why mTORC1 is a two-part dimer with its active sites hidden in clefts, and why mTORC2 ignores rapamycin.

The publication record shows Boehringer as a regular cryo-EM contributor to structural projects at ETH Zurich, many with Nenad Ban's group on ribosomes and their assembly. Since about 2020 the papers list the Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub of ETH Zurich, a shared facility, and include method work such as a 2020 study with Christopher Aylett's Imperial College group on transferring fragile support films for cryo-EM samples. No personal web page was opened, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Duran-Ortiz S.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (Athens, Ohio, USA)
Duran-Ortiz S.role: Researcher in John Kopchick's group at Ohio University who studies how switching off growth hormone action, even in middle age, lengthens life in mice
Duran-Ortiz S.sub: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (papers 2025–2026) · Edison Biotechnology Institute, Ohio University (papers from 2019)
story: Silvana Duran-Ortiz is first author of an Atlas study (DUR2026) that asked whether blocking growth hormone still helps if you wait until middle age. Mice born without the growth hormone receptor are small, very insulin sensitive and the longest-lived laboratory mice known, but that may be because they never grew normally. Here the team deleted the receptor at 12 months, when the mice were adults. Both sexes still lived significantly longer, without big changes in body size. Males also kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone structure as they aged, and the liver showed sex-specific changes in gene activity.

Growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1 and mTOR are linked growth signals, so the result fits the wider idea that turning growth signals down in adult life can slow ageing. It is a mouse study; in people, growth hormone receptor defects cause Laron syndrome, which is not the same as switching the receptor off in midlife.

Duran-Ortiz has published with the Ohio University growth hormone group of John Kopchick, Edward List and Darlene Berryman since at least 2019, first listed at the Edison Biotechnology Institute and more recently at the Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging. The work uses mice in which the growth hormone receptor is removed from the whole body or from single tissues such as fat, liver or muscle, and asks how each affects metabolism, immunity and lifespan; a 2026 paper found that old female mice without the receptor kept younger-looking B and T cell populations. No personal profile page was found, so the job title is not confirmed.

highlights.DUR2026: First author: showed that deleting the growth hormone receptor at 12 months of age still extends lifespan in both sexes of mice, with extra metabolic and muscle benefits in males.

Duran-Ortiz S.note: Previous story used 'her'; no source found for pronoun, removed. Title not confirmed.

Kidani Y.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Kidani Y.role: Researcher who, in Steven Bensinger's lab at UCLA, showed that activated killer T cells need SREBP-driven fat and cholesterol synthesis to expand
Kidani Y.sub: Steven Bensinger group, David Geffen School of Medicine, UCLA (papers 2011–2016, at the time of the study)
story: Yoko Kidani is first author of an Atlas study (KID2013) on what CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill virus-infected cells, need when they wake up. Within hours of activation they switch on genes for making fatty acids and cholesterol, the raw material for new cell membranes. The paper showed that this switch depends on SREBP proteins, the master regulators of lipid synthesis, and that the signal runs from PI3K through mTOR to SREBP: rapamycin given 30 minutes before stimulation blocked it in cells. T cells without SREBP activity could not grow and divide properly, and in mice infected with a virus they failed to expand.

The study is one of the clearest links between mTOR and immune cell metabolism. It helps explain why rapamycin and related drugs suppress the immune system: by blocking mTOR they also cut off the lipid supply that a dividing T cell needs. The key experiments were in mouse cells and mice.

Kidani worked in Steven Bensinger's group at the David Geffen School of Medicine, UCLA, where Bensinger, the senior author, studies how lipid metabolism shapes immune cells. Other papers from that period include a 2011 study with the same group on how liver X receptors help keep neutrophil numbers in balance. Later positions could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.KID2013: First author: showed that activated CD8 T cells need SREBP-driven lipid synthesis, switched on through PI3K and mTOR, to expand during viral infection.

Kidani Y.note: A Yoko Kidani at AstraZeneca K.K. Medical Affairs, Osaka (2021 diabetes paper, PMID 34962628) may be the same person but there is no second tie; left out.

Jung J.lab_name: Behrends Lab, Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine (Frankfurt am Main, Germany)
Jung J.role: Biochemist from Christian Behrends' group in Frankfurt who showed that the lysosomal amino acid transporter SLC38A9 helps switch on mTORC1, and who studied regulators of autophagy
Jung J.sub: Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine, Frankfurt (papers 2015–2019, Christian Behrends group; at the time of the study)
story: Jennifer Jung is first author of an Atlas study (JUN2015) in human cells about SLC38A9, a protein in the membrane of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the lysosome surface when amino acids are plentiful, with the help of the Rag GTPases and a scaffold called Ragulator. The study found SLC38A9 bound to the Rags and Ragulator. Removing SLC38A9 weakened mTORC1 activation by amino acids, and adding extra SLC38A9 made mTORC1 overactive. The same year two other groups reported similar findings, and SLC38A9 became known as a lysosomal arginine sensor for mTORC1.

Jung did this work in Christian Behrends' group at the Institute of Biochemistry II of Goethe University Frankfurt, which uses proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins and their partners, to map how autophagy and lysosomes are controlled. As first author of a 2017 eLife paper, Jung used an image-based RNAi screen to find autophagy regulators and showed that SMCR8, a partner of the ALS-linked protein C9ORF72, acts as a brake on the autophagy kinase ULK1. The publication record with the Behrends group runs from 2015 to 2019. Later positions could not be confirmed.

highlights.JUN2015: First author: showed that the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 binds the Rag-Ragulator machinery and is needed for full amino acid activation of mTORC1.

Jung J.note: Common surname; papers counted only when co-authored with Christian Behrends. Current position unknown.

de Araujo MEG.lab_name: Huber Lab, Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
de Araujo MEG.role: Cell biologist in Lukas Huber's group in Innsbruck who solved the crystal structure of the Ragulator (LAMTOR) complex, the lysosomal platform on which mTORC1 is switched on
de Araujo MEG.sub: Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (papers with Lukas Huber, 2004–2026)
story: Mariana de Araujo appears in three Atlas studies about the lysosome surface, where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on and off. In NAP2020 (cells and mice), mTORC1 was shown to reach the transcription factor TFEB by a special route that depends on the RagC and RagD proteins, and this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. In PRE2021 (cells), the stress-granule proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 were found to hold the TSC complex, a brake on mTORC1, on the lysosome. CUI2023 is a cryo-EM structure showing how two Rag-Ragulator units hand a TFEB molecule to the mTOR active site. De Araujo is a co-author in the middle of the author list on all three.

These collaborations build on de Araujo's own first-author work. In a 2017 Science paper from Innsbruck, de Araujo and colleagues solved the crystal structure of the human LAMTOR complex, also called Ragulator: five small proteins held together by LAMTOR1 that anchor the Rag GTPases to the lysosome and set their orientation for meeting mTORC1. The paper also showed which short stretches of LAMTOR1 are needed to recruit and hold the Rags. This structure is one of the reference points for how amino acid signals reach mTORC1.

De Araujo has published with Lukas Huber's group at the Medical University of Innsbruck since a 2004 study on the p14/MP1 scaffold, an earlier-known part of the same complex. The group studies how late endosomes and lysosomes organise signaling. In 2026 de Araujo was first author of a PNAS paper showing that the BORC complex, which moves lysosomes along the cell's tracks, can combine with subunits of a related complex, BLOC-1, to take on different transport jobs. No personal profile page was found, so the current job title is not confirmed.

highlights.NAP2020: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB through a RagC/D-dependent route that drives Birt-Hogg-Dube kidney disease.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author: contributed to the discovery that G3BP1 and G3BP2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes to restrain mTORC1.
highlights.CUI2023: Co-author: contributed to the cryo-EM structure of the mTORC1-TFEB-Rag-Ragulator megacomplex.

de Araujo MEG.note: Full name with initials 'Mariana E. G. de Araujo' from PubMed. Pronouns removed from old story (no source).

Stasyk T.lab_name: Huber Lab, Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
Stasyk T.role: Protein chemist in Lukas Huber's group in Innsbruck who has spent two decades applying proteomics to the late endosomes and lysosomes where mTORC1 is controlled
Stasyk T.sub: Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck (papers with Lukas Huber, 2004–2026)
story: Taras Stasyk is a co-author of two Atlas studies about mTORC1 control at the lysosome. REB2015 (cells) found that SLC38A9, a transporter in the lysosome membrane, is part of the machinery that senses amino acids and passes the signal to mTORC1. NAP2020 (cells and mice) showed that mTORC1 reaches the transcription factor TFEB by a special route that needs RagC and RagD, and that this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. Stasyk is in the middle of the author list on both.

Stasyk's main tool is proteomics, the use of mass spectrometry to identify which proteins are present in a sample and how they are modified. An early 2004 review with Lukas Huber described how to purify parts of the cell, such as organelles, before mass spectrometry so that rare signaling proteins can be seen. That approach suits the Huber lab's central question: which proteins sit on late endosomes and lysosomes and how they organise signals, including the LAMTOR (Ragulator) complex that anchors the Rag GTPases. Stasyk is also a co-author of the group's 2017 crystal structure of human LAMTOR.

The publication record shows Stasyk at the Medical University of Innsbruck from 2004 to 2026, most recently on a 2026 study of the lysosome transport complex BORC. No personal profile page was found, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

highlights.NAP2020: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB through a RagC/D-dependent route that drives Birt-Hogg-Dube kidney disease.
highlights.REB2015: Co-author: contributed to the identification of SLC38A9 as part of the lysosomal amino acid sensing machinery for mTORC1.

Al-Saadi RS.lab_name: Phillips Lab, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Eugene, Oregon, USA)
Al-Saadi RS.role: Worm biologist in Patrick Phillips' lab at the University of Oregon who studies how ageing differs between the sexes, using male C. elegans
Al-Saadi RS.sub: Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Patrick Phillips lab, papers 2025–2026) · Department of Biology, Syracuse University (Sarah Hall lab, 2026 paper)
story: Rose Al-Saadi is first author of ALS2026, a study in the tiny roundworm C. elegans. Most worm ageing research uses hermaphrodites, which make both eggs and sperm; this study looked at males. The team used a chemical switch (auxin-inducible degradation) to destroy DAF-2, the worm's insulin/IGF-1 receptor, throughout the body of adult males. Median lifespan rose by more than 440 percent, one of the largest lifespan gains reported for a single intervention, and the males stayed able to mate much later in life. Destroying DAF-2 only in the male germline, in contrast, shortened life, the opposite of what happens in hermaphrodites.

The insulin/IGF-1 pathway and mTOR are linked growth signals that both control ageing, so the paper shows that the sexes can respond differently to the same anti-ageing switch. The results are in worms and need testing in other animals.

Al-Saadi works with Patrick Phillips at the Institute of Ecology and Evolution of the University of Oregon on sex differences in ageing. A 2026 GeroScience paper from the pair tested seven compounds known to extend hermaphrodite lifespan: all lengthened male life, but only sulforaphane and metformin also kept males reproductively fit late in life. Earlier work in Sarah Hall's lab at Syracuse University, published in 2026, showed that a male worm's developmental history, including passage through the stress-resistant dauer stage, shapes how often worms cross-mate. No personal profile page was found, so the job title is not confirmed.

highlights.ALS2026: First author: showed that adult-wide degradation of the DAF-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor extends male C. elegans median lifespan by more than 440 percent and prolongs late-life mating.

Al-Saadi RS.note: ALS2026 has a bioRxiv preprint version (PMID 41278961). Syracuse affiliation suggests earlier PhD with Sarah Hall but degree not confirmed.

Zamboni N.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Zamboni N.role: Metabolomics specialist at ETH Zurich's Institute of Molecular Systems Biology whose mass spectrometry methods measure hundreds of metabolites at once, used in many collaborations on cell metabolism
Zamboni N.sub: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (papers 2016–2026; long-running work with Uwe Sauer)
story: Nicola Zamboni is a co-author of two Atlas studies that measured cell metabolism. GEI2016 tracked metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells and found that the amino acid L-arginine drops sharply after activation; raising L-arginine pushed the cells toward oxidative metabolism, made them live longer and improved their anti-tumor activity in a mouse model. DEM2026 found that losing the enzyme IDH3A in leukemic stem cells of acute myeloid leukemia slows the citric acid cycle and raises citrate, which switches on AMPK, turns down mTORC1 and makes the cells more sensitive to the drug venetoclax.

In both studies the key data came from metabolomics, the large-scale measurement of small molecules in cells. Zamboni's work at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology of ETH Zurich centres on mass spectrometry methods for measuring metabolites in cells. More than 30 papers are shared with Uwe Sauer, a systems biologist at the same institute, and PubMed lists over 160 papers on metabolomics from Zamboni, many of them collaborations in microbiology, immunology and cancer biology.
No personal profile page was opened, so the exact current title is not confirmed here; the affiliation on the 2026 Atlas paper is the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich.

highlights.GEI2016: Co-author: contributed metabolomics to the study showing that raised L-arginine shifts activated T cells to oxidative metabolism and improves their survival.
highlights.DEM2026: Co-author: contributed metabolite measurements to the study linking IDH3A loss, citrate build-up, AMPK activation and lower mTORC1 activity in AML stem cells.

sources: PubMed search Zamboni N[Author] AND Sauer U[Author]
Zamboni N.note: Title (likely senior scientist / group leader) not confirmed; web search budget ran out. Previous story used 'him'; removed.

Shi L.lab_name: Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Shi L.role: Immunologist at Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou whose group showed in mice that losing the lysosomal mTOR-activating protein Lamtor5 with age pushes macrophages into senescence and spreads inflammation
Shi L.sub: Key Laboratory of Artificial Organs and Computational Medicine, Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (papers 2024–2026)
story: Liyun Shi is senior author of an Atlas study (LV2026) on why the immune system ages. Lamtor5 is one of the five small proteins of the Ragulator complex, the platform on the lysosome surface where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. The team found that Lamtor5 levels fall with age in mouse macrophages, the immune cells that clean up debris and fight infection. Without enough Lamtor5 the macrophages became senescent, a state in which cells stop dividing but release inflammatory signals. The study traced this to the cGAS-STING pathway, an alarm system that senses DNA in the wrong place in the cell, and showed that the inflammation spread to other tissues. Restoring Lamtor5 in old mice reduced these signs of immune ageing.

The finding links a component of the mTOR machinery to inflammaging, the low-level chronic inflammation of old age. It is a mouse study, so whether Lamtor5 behaves the same way in human immune cells remains open.

PubMed lists Shi at the Institute of Translational Medicine of Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou on the Atlas paper and on a 2024 study, with clinical partners, of how gut bacteria and a population of macrophages drive bowel inflammation in children with glycogen storage disease type Ib. No official profile page was found, so the exact current title is not confirmed.

highlights.LV2026: Senior author: led the mouse study showing that age-related loss of Lamtor5 drives macrophage senescence and cGAS-STING inflammation, reversed by restoring Lamtor5.

Shi L.note: A Liyun Shi was corresponding author at the Key Laboratory of Inflammation and Immunoregulation, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (2019, PMID 31254739; gut inflammation and microbiota). Likely the same person given the topic, but no second tie, so left out of the story.

Lei HT.lab_name: Gonen Lab, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Lei HT.role: Structural biologist from Tamir Gonen's lab who solved crystal structures of the lysosomal arginine sensor SLC38A9, showing how it holds arginine and how its own tail plugs the binding pocket
Lei HT.sub: Tamir Gonen lab, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, Los Angeles (papers 2020–2023) · Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Ashburn, Virginia (papers 2018–2019)
story: Hsiang-Ting Lei is first author of LEI2018, the crystal structure of SLC38A9 from zebrafish with an arginine molecule bound. SLC38A9 is a transporter in the lysosome membrane that also acts as a sensor: when arginine builds up inside the lysosome, SLC38A9 helps tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that amino acids are plentiful. The structure, caught in a state open toward the cytosol, shows exactly where arginine sits and which parts of the protein grip it, giving a physical basis for arginine sensing.

In a 2020 follow-up in the journal Structure, again as first author, Lei solved a second SLC38A9 structure in which the protein's own N-terminal tail is inserted deep into the pocket where arginine normally binds. The team proposed a ball-and-chain model: when arginine is scarce the tail plugs the transporter, and when arginine is abundant the tail is pushed out and becomes free to activate the Rag GTPases and mTORC1.

Lei worked with Tamir Gonen, first at the Janelia Research Campus of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Ashburn, Virginia, where the lab also solved structures of an alanine transporter (2019), and then at HHMI at the University of California, Los Angeles, where Lei contributed to cryo-EM structures of the omega-3 fatty acid transporter Mfsd2a (2023). Later positions could not be confirmed.

highlights.LEI2018: First author: solved the crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9, the lysosomal arginine sensor for mTORC1.

Lei HT.note: lab_name changed from Janelia (Atlas paper affiliation) to the most recent confirmed affiliation (HHMI at UCLA, 2023). Current position unknown.

Robida-Stubbs S.lab_name: Blackwell Lab, Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Robida-Stubbs S.role: Researcher in Keith Blackwell's worm lab at the Joslin Diabetes Center who showed that TOR inhibition and rapamycin extend C. elegans lifespan through the protective factors SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO
Robida-Stubbs S.sub: Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Stem Cell Institute and Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School (T. Keith Blackwell group, papers 2012–2022)
story: Stacey Robida-Stubbs is first author of an Atlas study (ROB2012) on how blocking TOR lengthens life in the roundworm C. elegans. Lowering TORC1 genetically extended lifespan, and that needed two transcription factors that switch on defence genes: SKN-1, the worm version of Nrf, which protects against oxidative and chemical stress, and DAF-16, the worm FoxO. Rapamycin also extended lifespan, but needed only SKN-1, not DAF-16. The authors traced this difference to rapamycin also acting on TORC2. They also saw that rapamycin switched on a similar Nrf-type protective response in mice.

The paper showed that turning down TOR does more than slow growth: it actively switches on the cell's protective programmes. It also gave an early warning that rapamycin does not act like a pure TORC1 blocker, a theme the Atlas follows into mice and people.

The publication record places Robida-Stubbs in T. Keith Blackwell's group at the Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School from 2012 to at least 2022, including a 2022 Nature Communications paper showing that the stress factor ATF-4 and hydrogen sulfide production help explain why lowering protein synthesis or mTORC1 extends worm lifespan. No profile page was found, so the current role is not confirmed.

highlights.ROB2012: First author: showed in C. elegans that TORC1 inhibition extends lifespan through SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO, while rapamycin's effect needs only SKN-1.

Robida-Stubbs S.note: A 'Stacey Robida' (Stacey I. Robida) published on insulin-stimulated GLUT4 trafficking in Michael Czech's lab at UMass Medical School (2002, 2004; PMIDs 12490950, 15169906). Possibly the same person before a name change, but not confirmed; left out.

Xiao T.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Xiao T.role: Researcher at the Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study and first author of a 2026 review on how nutrient-sensing pathways steer adult stem cells through life
Xiao T.sub: School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (at the time of the study)
story: Tianxiong Xiao is first author of XIA2026, a review in Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology. It does not report new experiments. It pulls together evidence that four nutrient-sensing systems, mTOR, AMPK, the sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signaling, work as one network to decide what adult stem cells do: stay at rest (quiescence), wake up and divide, or turn into specialised cells. Adult stem cells keep tissues such as blood, muscle, gut and brain supplied with new cells, so this decision matters throughout life.

The review argues that with age the network drifts out of balance, for example with mTOR too active, which can wear stem cells out and add to tissue decline. Because it is a review, its framework is a proposal built on mostly animal and cell studies, and the Atlas treats it as a map of ideas rather than as evidence in its own right.

PubMed lists Xiao at the Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Hu C as senior author. No other papers could be tied to this person with confidence, and no profile page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.XIA2026: First author: wrote the review proposing that mTOR, AMPK, sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signaling form one network steering adult stem cell fate and ageing.

Xiao T.note: Common surname; no further identity-confirmed papers. Career path unknown.

Paul D.lab_name: Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Paul D.role: Cell cycle researcher in Steven Cappell's lab at the National Cancer Institute who found that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C to give cells a burst of glycolysis as they start to divide
Paul D.sub: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Steven Cappell lab, papers 2021–2025)
story: Debasish Paul is first author of PAU2025, a Nature paper about the moment a resting cell decides to divide. When a growth signal arrives, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to CDH1, the helper protein of a large enzyme called APC/C that tags other proteins for destruction. This partly releases CDH1 and briefly switches APC/C off. One of APC/C's usual targets, the glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3, then builds up, and the cell burns more glucose for a while, until a slower-acting phosphatase turns APC/C back on. The study, in human cells, showed that this short pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle.

The finding gives mTOR a new job: besides boosting protein synthesis, it times a metabolic switch by reaching into the cell-cycle machinery. Because many cancers have overactive mTOR, the circuit may also help explain how tumor cells keep their fuel supply high, although the paper itself did not test tumors.

The publication record places Paul in Steven Cappell's lab at the Center for Cancer Research of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda from at least 2021, when the group published a study showing that cells hit by DNA damage early in the cycle often keep going rather than stopping at the classic checkpoint. The lab uses time-lapse imaging of single living cells to follow cell-cycle decisions. No profile page was found, so the current role is not confirmed.

highlights.PAU2025: First author: showed that mTOR phosphorylates CDH1 to briefly inactivate APC/C, letting PFKFB3 build up and boost glycolysis as cells enter the cell cycle.

Paul D.note: A Debasish Paul at the National Centre for Cell Science, Pune (2019, F-box protein FBXO16 and beta-catenin, PMID 30714168) may be the same person (ubiquitin ligase biology) but there is no second tie; left out. Other PubMed 'Debasish Paul' entries (chemistry, IIT Dhanbad) are different people.

Lee JH.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology, University of Michigan Medical School (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Lee JH.role: Physiologist at the University of Michigan who first showed in flies that Sestrin is a feedback brake on TOR that protects against age-related decline, and has since studied Sestrins as stress-induced regulators of mTORC1
Lee JH.sub: Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology, University of Michigan Medical School (papers 2016–2022) · Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, University of California San Diego (Michael Karin lab, 2010 paper)
story: Jun Hee Lee is first author of LEE2010, a Science paper from Michael Karin's laboratory at the University of California San Diego. In fruit flies, the team found that Sestrin levels rise when TOR stays active, and that Sestrin then pushes TOR back down by switching on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor. This makes Sestrin a feedback brake. Flies without Sestrin built up fat and developed mitochondrial damage, muscle weakness and heart problems that looked like early ageing. Treating them with rapamycin or with an AMPK activator prevented these problems.

The paper put Sestrins on the map of ageing research. Later work by other groups showed that in mammals Sestrin2 binds the amino acid leucine and passes that signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex, so Sestrins are now seen as both stress sensors and nutrient sensors for mTORC1.

Lee moved to the University of Michigan, where PubMed lists the Department of Molecular and Integrative Physiology of the Medical School. Lee's group there continued the Sestrin work, including a 2016 review on the biochemical basis of Sestrin activity, which describes Sestrins as stress-induced proteins that hold down both reactive oxygen species and mTORC1, and a 2022 commentary with Robert Wessells on how Sestrin links exercise to body temperature control. No profile page was opened, so the current title is not confirmed.

highlights.LEE2010: First author: showed in fruit flies that Sestrin acts as a feedback inhibitor of TOR and that its loss causes age-like fat, mitochondrial, muscle and heart defects that TOR inhibition prevents.

Lee JH.note: Very common surname: Michigan identity rests on full name 'Jun Hee Lee' plus the specific Sestrin-mTORC1-ageing topic as corresponding author; no direct link (e.g., Karin co-authorship) was checked. Curator may want to verify on the Michigan faculty page.
